common_name: Lady Banks Rose (Thornless Climbing Heirloom Rose)

planting.note: Plant container roses in spring against a strong, large support such as an arbor, pergola, or fence, since Lady Banks eventually becomes an enormous, vigorous climber; it is thornless and blooms only once in spring but very heavily.

directions: Plant against a substantial support in well-drained soil in full sun. A Southern heirloom favorite introduced from China in the early 1800s, Lady Banks Rose is a nearly thornless, extremely vigorous climber that can eventually cover an entire arbor, porch, or old tree with a spectacular single spring flush of small, rosette-shaped flowers, typically pale yellow or white depending on the form grown, often accompanied by a light violet fragrance. Unlike repeat-blooming modern roses, it flowers only once a year but with such abundance that a mature plant can be smothered in thousands of blooms for several weeks. It is remarkably drought-tolerant and pest-free once established, needs only occasional pruning right after bloom to control its size, and is a classic sight on old homes throughout the Gulf South.

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, acidic, well-drained soil in partial shade to morning sun; Encore azaleas rebloom in summer and fall in addition to their main spring flush, unlike most traditional azaleas that flower only once.

directions: Plant in moist, acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade to morning sun, protecting plants from harsh afternoon sun in the hottest part of zone 9 summers. The Encore breeding series, developed in Louisiana beginning in the 1990s, was a breakthrough because it combined the classic look of Southern azaleas with genuine repeat blooming, flowering not just in the traditional spring flush but again in summer and often into fall, greatly extending the color season of a plant long associated with a single brief burst of spring bloom. Dozens of named Encore cultivars are now available across a wide range of flower colors and mature sizes, all sharing the reblooming trait and reasonably good heat tolerance for the Gulf South. Water deeply during dry spells, especially heading into the summer and fall bloom flushes, and prune lightly right after the spring bloom to shape without removing the buds that will produce later color.

common_name: Louis Philippe Rose (Classic Deep South Heirloom China Rose)

planting.note: Plant container or bare-root roses in spring in well-drained soil in full sun; Louis Philippe is an old Deep South China rose that blooms nearly continuously in the long growing season of the Gulf Coast and needs very little winter protection in zone 8-9.

directions: Plant in well-drained, average soil in full sun. Introduced from China in the 1830s and long naturalized around old homesites and cemeteries across the Deep South, Louis Philippe is a classic 'found rose,' still turning up growing untended for a century or more with little care, testament to its exceptional heat tolerance, disease resistance, and toughness. It produces rich crimson-red, cupped, moderately fragrant blooms almost continuously through the long, hot Gulf Coast growing season, a trait that made China roses like this one especially valuable to Southern gardeners long before modern repeat-blooming roses existed. It thrives on neglect, needs only an occasional shaping prune, and is highly resistant to the black spot and powdery mildew that trouble many modern hybrid roses in humid climates.

common_name: Old Blush Rose (Parson's Pink China, One of the Oldest Cultivated Roses)

planting.note: Plant container or bare-root roses in spring in well-drained soil in full sun; Old Blush is one of the original four China roses introduced to Europe in the 1750s-1790s and is credited with bringing repeat bloom into modern rose breeding.

directions: Plant in well-drained, average soil in full sun. Old Blush is one of the four founding China roses brought to Europe in the late 1700s and is historically significant as one of the first roses to introduce genuine repeat bloom to Western rose breeding, which until then relied on once-blooming European roses. It produces semi-double, silvery-pink flowers that deepen in color with age and heat, blooming in flushes nearly continuously through the growing season, and remains a tough, easygoing garden rose with excellent heat tolerance and good resistance to black spot. Grown for over two centuries across the Gulf South, it needs little more than an occasional shaping prune and is a good choice for gardeners who want an authentic heirloom with real historical rose-breeding significance.
